blocks.text:
Every thread of a process shares the same address space. Two threads that read and write the same variable without coordination produce results that depend on the exact interleaving of their instructions, and the operating system scheduler, not the programmer, decides that interleaving. A defect of this kind is called a race condition. It is the root cause of lost updates, duplicate database rows, corrupted data structures and, indirectly, of every deadlock discussed later in this Part.

This chapter defines the problem precisely, states the properties that any solution must have, and describes the hardware primitives (atomic read-modify-write instructions, compare-and-swap and memory barriers) on which every lock, semaphore and concurrent collection is built. All experiments were run on a Linux 6.18 virtual machine with 2 CPUs and OpenJDK 21.0.12; JDK 25 behaves identically for the examples shown unless stated otherwise.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Race condition and data race

A **race condition** is a flaw in which the correctness of a computation depends on the relative timing of events in several threads. A **data race** is the narrower, mechanically detectable case: two threads access the same memory location, at least one access is a write, and no synchronisation orders the accesses. A program can contain a race condition without a data race (two correctly locked updates may still happen in the wrong order for the business rule), and a data race is always a defect in languages with a defined memory model: it is undefined behaviour in C11 and a source of unspecified (though memory-safe) results in the Java Memory Model.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: A critical section A critical section is a region of code that accesses a shared resource and must not be executed by more than one thread at a time. Protecting it with mutual exclusion makes the sequence of instructions inside it appear to execute as one indivisible step to every other thread.

#### Why counter++ is not one step

The statement `counter++` looks atomic in source code. In machine code it is a read-modify-write sequence of three operations: load the value into a register, add one, store the register back. The JVM bytecode shows the same structure:

blocks.code:
$ javap -c -p Counter
  static void inc();
    Code:
       0: getstatic     #7                  // Field count:I
       3: iconst_1
       4: iadd
       5: putstatic     #7                  // Field count:I
       8: return
blocks.title: Bytecode of a static counter increment

blocks.text: Between the load and the store, the thread may be preempted, or another CPU core may execute its own load of the same, not yet updated, value. Both threads then compute the same result and both store it; one increment disappears. This is a **lost update**.

blocks.text:
#### Requirements for a solution

A correct protocol for entering and leaving a critical section must satisfy three requirements, formulated in the classical operating-systems literature:

- **Mutual exclusion.** At most one thread is inside the critical section at any time.
- **Progress.** If no thread is inside and some threads wish to enter, the choice of the next thread depends only on those threads and cannot be postponed indefinitely.
- **Bounded waiting.** After a thread has requested entry, only a bounded number of other threads can enter before it does. This excludes starvation.

No assumption may be made about relative CPU speeds or the number of processors. A solution that works only on one core, or only when threads are fair, is not a solution.

#### Hardware support: atomic instructions

Pure software protocols exist (Dekker, Peterson) but they assume that memory operations become visible in program order, which modern CPUs do not guarantee. Practical systems rely on instructions that perform a read-modify-write on one memory location as a single indivisible step with respect to all other cores:

blocks.caption: Atomic read-modify-write primitives (x86-64 and AArch64 shown).

blocks.text:
On x86 the `lock` prefix makes the instruction atomic and also acts as a full memory barrier. On older ARM cores atomicity is built from a load-linked/store-conditional pair: `ldxr` loads and marks the address, `stxr` stores only if no other core wrote the address in the meantime, and the sequence is retried on failure.

#### Compare-and-swap

**Compare-and-swap** (CAS) takes an address, an expected value and a new value. If the memory still holds the expected value, the new value is stored and the operation reports success; otherwise nothing is stored and failure is reported. All of this is one atomic step. A CAS loop builds an arbitrary update from it: read the current value, compute the new value from it, attempt the CAS, and retry from the read if it failed.

blocks.text:
`java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` compiles to a single `lock xadd` on x86; `AtomicInteger.updateAndGet(f)` and `compareAndSet` use the CAS loop directly. CAS has one well-known weakness, the **ABA problem**: a location holding A is changed to B and back to A, and a CAS that expected A succeeds although the state changed in between. For counters this is harmless; for pointer-based structures it is solved by pairing the value with a version stamp (`AtomicStampedReference`).

#### Memory ordering and barriers

Atomicity solves only half of the problem. Modern processors and compilers reorder memory operations for speed, and each core keeps pending stores in a **store buffer** before they reach the shared cache. As a result, another core can observe the effects of one thread in an order that no sequential reading of the source code predicts.

blocks.text: x86-64 implements a comparatively strong model (total store order) in which only the reordering of a store followed by a load to a different address is visible. ARM and POWER permit many more reorderings. A **memory barrier** (fence) instruction restricts reordering: stores before the barrier become visible before loads and stores after it. Higher-level primitives hide this: acquiring a mutex acts as an acquire barrier and releasing it as a release barrier, so everything written inside a critical section is visible to the next thread that acquires the same lock. In Java the same guarantees are expressed as happens-before edges: unlock then lock of the same monitor, a write then a read of the same `volatile` field, `Thread.start` and `Thread.join`. Part 4 later returns to these edges when thread dumps and `volatile` misuse are discussed; the full model is specified in the Java Memory Model chapter of the Java Language Specification.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: `volatile` guarantees visibility and ordering, not atomicity. A `volatile int` incremented with `++` still performs a separate read and write. In the experiment of this chapter a volatile counter lost between 8 and 32 percent of 10 million increments, depending on the run. Use `AtomicInteger`, `LongAdder` or a lock when the update depends on the previous value.

### Worked trace

The table follows the interleaving of the previous figure instruction by instruction. The counter starts at 41; thread A and thread B each execute `counter++` once. The notation `rA` and `rB` denotes a register private to each thread.

rows: B reads the same old value
B overwrites with the same value
blocks.caption: Step-by-step lost update (counter starts at 41).

blocks.text:
Two increments were requested and the value rose by one. With a mutex around steps 1 to 5 of each thread, thread B cannot execute its load until thread A has stored, and the final value is 43. With an atomic fetch-and-add, steps 1 to 3 collapse into one indivisible instruction with the same result.

### Hands-on

#### A race in C

The program creates two POSIX threads that each increment a shared `long` one million times without synchronisation. It is compiled with `-O0` so that the compiler keeps the load, add and store visible in the machine code.

blocks.title: race.c

blocks.text: The disassembly of the worker loop shows the three steps, with the counter in memory between each of them:

blocks.code:
$ objdump -d race | grep -A12 "<worker>:" | sed -n 9,13p
    11be:       48 8b 05 53 2e 00 00    mov    0x2e53(%rip),%rax        # 4018 <counter>
    11c5:       48 83 c0 01             add    $0x1,%rax
    11c9:       48 89 05 48 2e 00 00    mov    %rax,0x2e48(%rip)        # 4018 <counter>
blocks.title: Disassembly of the increment (typical output)

blocks.text: Four consecutive runs lost between 41 and 49 percent of the increments, and no two runs agreed:

blocks.code:
$ gcc -O0 -pthread -o race race.c && for i in 1 2 3 4; do ./race; done
expected 2000000, got 1175080
expected 2000000, got 1042279
expected 2000000, got 1073544
expected 2000000, got 1028390
blocks.title: Unsynchronised increments, four runs (typical output)

blocks.text:
With optimisation (`-O2`) the compiler may keep `counter` in a register for the whole loop and write it back once; the program is then still wrong, but wrong in a different way. This illustrates why a data race is undefined behaviour: the compiler is entitled to assume that it does not occur.

#### Two correct fixes in C

The next program runs the same workload twice: once guarded by a `pthread_mutex_t` and once through a C11 atomic with `atomic_fetch_add`.

blocks.title: fix.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -O0 -pthread -o fix fix.c && ./fix && ./fix
mutex   result=2000000  time=139 ms
atomic  result=2000000  time=39 ms
mutex   result=2000000  time=126 ms
atomic  result=2000000  time=36 ms
blocks.title: Mutex and atomic versions (measured on the build machine, typical)

blocks.text:
Both versions are correct; the atomic is roughly three to four times faster here because the single `lock xadd` instruction never enters the kernel and never sleeps. The mutex is not slow in itself (an uncontended lock is also a user-space atomic), but two threads that collide on it pay for queueing and futex calls, described in the next chapter.

#### The same experiment in Java

blocks.title: RaceDemo.java

blocks.text: Run on the build machine, the unsafe variants lost updates in most runs, while the three safe variants always produced 10,000,000:

blocks.code:
$ java RaceDemo.java
plain int    19 ms
volatile     266 ms
synchronized 475 ms
AtomicInt    65 ms
LongAdder    124 ms
plain        = 10000000
volatile     = 7098011
synchronized = 10000000
AtomicInt    = 10000000
LongAdder    = 10000000
blocks.title: RaceDemo, one typical run

blocks.text:
In this particular run the plain `int` was correct; in other runs of the same program it ended at 9993835 and 9980288. That variability is the defining property of a race: the defective run may pass every test and fail in production. Two further observations follow from the numbers. First, the JIT compiler may keep the plain field in a register, which makes the unsafe loop very fast and the loss rare in short runs. Second, the volatile counter lost far more, because every increment is forced to memory where the two cores constantly interfere. A `LongAdder` is slower than an `AtomicInteger` in this two-thread test because it is designed for many threads: it spreads contention over several cells and sums them on read.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: duplicate orders from a check-then-act sequence

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot order service runs three replicas behind a load balancer. The handler checks whether an order with the client-supplied request identifier already exists and, if not, inserts it. A mobile client retries after a timeout, and the retry reaches a second replica while the first request is still in flight.

**Symptoms.** Customers receive two confirmation e-mails and two shipments for one purchase. The error rate is zero; no exception appears in any log. Support tickets cluster in periods of network latency.

**Diagnosis.** The duplicates are visible in the database as soon as the right question is asked. Rows sharing a request identifier prove that the application check did not serialise the two requests:

blocks.code:
$ psql orders -c "SELECT request_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY request_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1"
 request_id | count
------------+-------
 req-42     |     2
blocks.title: Finding duplicates (illustrative query; output typical)

blocks.text: Application locks cannot explain or repair this: a `synchronized` block protects one JVM, while three replicas run three JVMs. The reproduction below uses SQLite and five threads, each with its own connection, to model five concurrent requests. Each thread executes the check, waits 50 ms (network and service latency) and then inserts.

blocks.title: orders.py

blocks.code:
$ python3 orders.py
unique index=False rows in orders=5  inserted=5 rejected=0
unique index=True  rows in orders=1  inserted=1 rejected=4
atomic UPDATE=False copies sold=5 (stock was 1)
atomic UPDATE=True  copies sold=1 (stock was 1)
blocks.title: Reproduction of the race and of both fixes (measured)

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** A check-then-act sequence executed as two separate database statements. The check and the act are not one atomic step, so the window between them is a critical section that no lock protects. The stock example shows the same defect as a read-modify-write: five buyers each read quantity 1 and each decrement it.

**Fix.** Immediate: delete the duplicate rows and, if payments are affected, reconcile them. Permanent: let the database arbitrate. Declare `UNIQUE (request_id)`, treat the resulting constraint violation (`DataIntegrityViolationException` in Spring) as "already processed" and return the stored order. For inventory, replace the read-modify-write by one conditional statement, `UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty > 0`, and check that exactly one row was updated. Where a transaction spans several statements, use a locking read (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) or an isolation level that prevents the anomaly, after confirming how the chosen database implements it. **Prevention.** Require an idempotency key on every state-changing endpoint, enforce uniqueness in the schema, add a concurrent integration test that fires the same request from several threads, and alert on `GROUP BY ... HAVING` `COUNT(*) > 1` queries run periodically against business keys.

#### Incident: under-counting metrics in a singleton bean

**Scenario.** A controller in a Spring application keeps `private int requestCount` in a field and increments it per request. Spring beans are singletons, so every Tomcat worker thread shares the field.

**Symptoms.** The dashboard built from the field reports 9,980,288 requests while the access log, the load balancer and the database all agree on 10,000,000. The discrepancy varies from one deployment to the next and grows with traffic.

**Diagnosis.** Comparing an independent count (access-log lines, `wc -l`) with the application counter shows a deficit that is never negative. A deficit that appears only under concurrent load, never under a single-threaded test, and differs between runs is the signature of lost updates. The `RaceDemo` run above reproduces the same pattern: the plain counter ended at 9980288 in one run and at 10000000 in another.

**Root cause.** A non-atomic increment of shared mutable state by multiple threads, with no happens-before relationship between them.

**Fix.** Immediate: restart does not help; accept the metric as approximate. Permanent: replace the field by a `java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder`, or, preferably, by a Micrometer `Counter`, which is already thread-safe.

**Prevention.** Treat every mutable field of a singleton as shared. Prefer immutable beans and thread-safe types; run static analysis or review for non-final fields in `@Component`, `@Service` and `@Controller` classes.

### Questions to expect

1. **What is a race condition, and how does it differ from a data race?** A race condition is incorrect behaviour that depends on thread timing. A data race is two unsynchronised accesses to one location, at least one a write. A program can have either without the other.
2. **Why is** `i++` **not thread-safe even for an** `int`**?** It is a load, an add and a store. Two threads can load the same value and both store the same result, losing one update. Only a lock or an atomic read-modify-write makes it indivisible.
3. **What three properties must a critical-section solution have?** Mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
4. **How does compare-and-swap work, and what is the ABA problem?** CAS atomically stores a new value only if the location still holds the expected value. ABA occurs when the value changes from A to B and back to A, so a CAS succeeds although the state changed; version stamps solve it.
5. **Does** `volatile` **make** `counter++` **safe?** No. It makes each read and write visible and ordered, but the increment remains two separate operations. In the experiment it lost up to about 32 percent of the increments in a run.
6. **When is** `AtomicInteger` **preferable to** `synchronized`**, and when is it not?** For a single variable updated independently it is simpler and avoids blocking. When an invariant spans several variables, a lock is required because CAS protects one location only.
7. **Why can a lock in a Java service not prevent duplicate orders across replicas?** The lock lives in one JVM. State shared across processes must be arbitrated by a shared system, normally the database through unique constraints or conditional updates.
8. **What does a memory barrier do?** It limits reordering of memory operations around it, so that stores before it become visible before loads and stores after it. Lock acquire and release imply the necessary barriers.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A race condition arises when correctness depends on the interleaving of threads; `counter++` is three steps (load, add, store), so concurrent increments lose updates.
- A critical-section solution needs mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting, and cannot assume anything about CPU speed.
- Atomic read-modify-write instructions (`lock xadd`, `lock cmpxchg`, `xchg`) are the hardware basis of all locks and atomics; CAS loops build lock-free updates.
- Memory barriers constrain the reordering caused by store buffers and compilers; lock operations and `volatile` provide them, but `volatile` does not provide atomicity.
- Races are nondeterministic: a test may pass for months. Reproduce them with many threads and long loops, and fix them structurally (unique constraints, atomics, immutable state).

sections.title: Mutexes, Semaphores, Condition Variables and Spinlocks

blocks.text:
A critical section needs an entry protocol, and the thread that finds the section occupied needs a policy: wait by repeatedly testing, or give up the CPU until the section is free. The operating system and the C library provide a small family of synchronisation primitives that implement these policies. The same primitives underlie Java: `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, `Semaphore` and `Condition` are all built on the mechanisms described here, and every contended Java lock ends in a Linux system call named `futex`.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Mutex

A **mutex** (mutual-exclusion lock) has two operations, lock and unlock, and an owner. The thread that locked it must unlock it. A thread that finds the mutex held is put to sleep by the kernel and woken when the mutex is released, so a waiting thread consumes no CPU time. POSIX offers several types: the default (normal) mutex, whose behaviour on self-deadlock or on unlock by a non-owner is undefined; the error-checking mutex, which returns an error; and the recursive mutex, which counts nested locks by the same thread. Java's `synchronized` and `ReentrantLock` are recursive.

#### Spinlock

A **spinlock** is a lock whose waiters do not sleep: they loop on an atomic test-and-set until the lock is free. The wait costs CPU cycles but avoids the context switch. It is appropriate when the critical section is shorter than a context switch, when the holder cannot be preempted, and when at least as many CPUs as contenders exist. These conditions hold inside the Linux kernel, where a spinlock holder runs with preemption (and often interrupts) disabled, and rarely hold in ordinary user programs. If a user-space thread holding a spinlock is preempted, every spinning thread burns its whole time slice without progress, as the measurement later in this chapter shows.

blocks.text:
#### Semaphore

A **semaphore**, introduced by Dijkstra, is a non-negative integer with two atomic operations. `wait` (P) decrements the integer and blocks while it is zero. `post` (V) increments it and wakes one waiter. A semaphore initialised to 1 acts as a mutex, but it has no owner: any thread may post, which makes semaphores suitable for signalling between threads ("one item is now available") and unsuitable for protecting data against accidental unlocking. A counting semaphore initialised to N limits concurrency to N, which is the model of a connection pool or of `java.util.concurrent.Semaphore`.

#### Condition variable and monitor

A mutex answers "may I enter?" but not "has the state I need arrived?". A **condition variable** lets a thread wait for a predicate on shared state. `wait(cond, mutex)` atomically releases the mutex and sleeps; on wake-up it reacquires the mutex before returning. `signal` wakes one waiter and `broadcast` wakes all. Three rules apply in every language:

- The predicate is always tested in a `while` loop, never an `if`. A wake-up does not guarantee that the predicate is true: another thread may have consumed the state first, and POSIX permits spurious wake-ups.
- The state change and the signal are made while holding the same mutex that the waiter uses, which prevents a signal from falling between the waiter's test and its sleep (a lost wake-up).
- `broadcast` is the safe default when waiters wait for different predicates on one condition variable.

A **monitor** packages a mutex with its condition variables and the data they guard. Java builds a monitor into every object: `synchronized` is the lock, `wait`, `notify` and `notifyAll` are the condition operations.

#### How a mutex is implemented: the futex

Entering the kernel for every lock operation would make locking expensive, and the great majority of lock operations are uncontended. Linux therefore implements the mutex in two layers, joined by the **futex** ("fast user-space mutex") system call. The lock state is one 32-bit integer in user memory. The fast path is an atomic instruction on that integer and involves no kernel. Only a thread that must sleep, or a thread that releases a lock that has sleepers, calls `futex`. The two operations used by mutexes are:

- `FUTEX_WAIT(addr, expected)`: if the integer at `addr` still equals `expected`, put the caller to sleep on a kernel queue keyed by that address; otherwise return immediately. The re-check, performed under the kernel's own lock, closes the race between a thread deciding to sleep and another thread releasing the lock.
- `FUTEX_WAKE(addr, n)`: wake at most `n` threads sleeping on `addr`.

The glibc normal mutex encodes three states in the word: 0 (unlocked), 1 (locked, no waiters), 2 (locked, waiters may exist). The flag `FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG` marks a futex shared only by threads of one process, which lets the kernel skip the cross-process address lookup.

blocks.text:
Condition variables, semaphores and the parking primitives of the JVM use the same system call with different words and different protocols; only the mutex word is described here.

### Classical synchronisation problems

#### Bounded buffer (producer and consumer)

Producers add items to a buffer of fixed capacity, consumers remove them. A producer must wait when the buffer is full, a consumer when it is empty, and access to the buffer indices must be exclusive. The standard solution uses two counting semaphores, `empty` (free slots, initially the capacity) and `full` (filled slots, initially 0), plus one mutex for the indices. The order of the semaphore wait before the mutex matters: reversing it lets a producer hold the mutex while it sleeps for a free slot that only a consumer, blocked on that mutex, could create, which is a deadlock.

blocks.text: The following C program runs one producer and one consumer over four slots and verifies the sum of 100,000 items.

blocks.text:
With a four-slot buffer the two threads alternate constantly and almost every operation sleeps and wakes a thread. Under `strace -f -c -e trace=futex` the same run recorded 182,870 futex calls (the tracer slows the program but does not change the count order of magnitude). This is why throughput-sensitive systems use larger buffers or batch several items per hand-off.

In Java the same structure uses a lock with two conditions. The listing shows the rules above: both predicates are tested in `while` loops and the signal is sent while the lock is held.

blocks.text:
#### Readers and writers

Many threads may read a structure simultaneously, but a writer needs exclusive access. A read-write lock allows any number of concurrent readers or one writer. The policy question is fairness: reader preference can starve writers, writer preference can starve readers. `ReentrantReadWriteLock` in its default non-fair mode blocks a new reader when a writer is first in the queue, as the timeline shows for R3.

blocks.text: The program below has one writer that updates two fields `a` and `b` non-atomically (the invariant is `a == b`) and two readers that check the invariant. Without the lock readers observe the half-updated state constantly; with the read-write lock they never do.

blocks.text:
#### Dining philosophers

Five philosophers sit at a round table with one fork between each pair of neighbours. Each needs both adjacent forks to eat. If every philosopher takes the left fork first, all can hold one fork and wait forever for the other: the system is deadlocked. The problem models a set of threads that each need two locks.

The ordered solution is deadlock-free and every philosopher eats the same number of times in this run; it does not by itself guarantee fairness, which would require an additional mechanism such as a fair lock.

### Worked trace

The following trace shows the futex protocol on a real mutex. The program creates three threads that each take the same mutex 200 times and sleep 500 microseconds while holding it, so the lock is contended on almost every acquisition.

blocks.title: futex2.c

blocks.text: First the uncontended case: one thread, 200,000 lock and unlock pairs. Then the contended case: three threads, 200 iterations each, summarised with `strace -c`.

blocks.text: The single-threaded run performed 200,000 lock and unlock pairs with one futex call in total, which belongs to thread start-up. The contended run needed 1,120 futex calls for 600 critical sections, almost two per section: one `FUTEX_WAIT` by a loser and one `FUTEX_WAKE` by the owner. rows: Thread 1394 found the word nonzero, set it to 2 and sleeps: expected value 2, no timeout.
Thread 1393 unlocks: the word was 2, so it wakes one sleeper; the return value 1 reports one thread woken.
Thread 1394 acquires, then on the next iteration waits again; thread 1393 wakes it again.
Thread 1393 finishes its last iteration and exits.
Thread 1394 unlocks with state 2 left by its earlier contention; no sleeper remains, so the wake returns 0.

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

#### Cost of the fast path

Without tracing, one thread performing two million lock and unlock pairs of a `pthread_mutex_t` finished in 33 ms of user time, about 16 ns per pair, and no system time: the uncontended path never enters the kernel. Four threads performing the same total work took 112 ms elapsed and 63 ms of system time, spent mostly in futex calls. Contention converts a user-space operation into a kernel operation.

#### Spinlock against mutex

The program `spin.c` runs the same increment under a test-and-set spinlock and under a mutex and performs a fixed amount of busy work inside the critical section (an inner loop of 2,000 iterations). The machine has 2 CPUs.

blocks.title: spin.c

blocks.code:
$ for n in 2 4 8; do ./spin $n 20000 2000; done
threads=2 mutex    counter=40000     209 ms
threads=2 spinlock counter=40000     313 ms
threads=4 mutex    counter=80000     360 ms
threads=4 spinlock counter=80000     914 ms
threads=8 mutex    counter=160000     753 ms
threads=8 spinlock counter=160000    4229 ms
blocks.title: Spinlock against mutex on 2 CPUs (measured on a shared, loaded VM; typical)

blocks.text:
With as many threads as CPUs the two locks are comparable. With more threads than CPUs the spinlock degrades by a factor of 2.5 at four threads and 5.6 at eight: the kernel preempts a thread that holds the lock, and every other thread then spins through its whole time slice (several milliseconds) before the holder runs again. The mutex waiters sleep, so the CPU goes to the holder immediately. The lesson is general: user-space spinning is justified only with a guarantee that the holder is running.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: 100 percent CPU from a spin-wait loop

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot batch component waits for a background initialisation task by polling a flag in a tight loop (`while (!ready) { }`), written to avoid the cost of a lock. The service is deployed to Kubernetes with a CPU limit of one core.

**Symptoms.** CPU utilisation sits at the limit within seconds of start-up and does not fall; request latency is high because the throttled container shares its single core between the spinning thread and the request threads. Heap and garbage collection are normal.

**Diagnosis.** The first question is which thread consumes the CPU. `top -H` lists threads instead of processes; the thread id in its first column is the Linux thread id, and `jcmd` prints the same number as `nid` in the thread dump (decimal on JDK 21; JDK 17 and earlier print it in hexadecimal, so convert with `printf '%x'`).

blocks.code:
$ top -H -b -n1 -p 9117 | sed -n 7,10p

 9118 root      20   0 4154288  97156  34896 S   0.0   1.2   0:00.46 java
$ jcmd 9117 Thread.print | grep -A6 '"spinner"'
"spinner" #25 [9142] daemon prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=4627.50ms elapsed=4.69s tid=0x... nid=9142 runnable

        at StateDemo.lambda$main$6(StateDemo.java:24)

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** Busy-waiting on a condition, which keeps a CPU occupied for a wait whose duration depends on an external event.

**Fix.** Immediate: restart does not cure it; raising the CPU limit only hides it. Permanent: replace the loop by a blocking construct: `CountDownLatch`, `CompletableFuture.get()`, a `BlockingQueue` or `Object.wait()` in a loop. Where a very short spin is justified, call `Thread.onSpinWait()` inside the loop and bound the number of iterations before parking.

**Prevention.** Alert on per-thread CPU (a single thread at 100 percent for minutes), review any `while` loop whose body is empty, and take a thread dump whenever CPU is high without matching traffic.

#### Incident: throughput falls after a deploy because a lock is held too long

**Scenario.** A release adds audit logging inside an existing `synchronized` method that updates a shared in-memory ledger. The log call formats a string and writes to a file, which is several orders of magnitude slower than the update it sits next to. Eight Tomcat threads call the method.

**Symptoms.** Throughput does not scale with load, p99 latency rises with concurrency, and CPU use remains below the machine capacity although requests queue. Adding replicas helps only linearly with cost. **Diagnosis.** CPU below capacity with high latency means that threads wait rather than compute. A thread dump shows how they wait: one thread holds the monitor and does the slow work, the others sit in the entry list.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The critical section contains work that does not need protection (formatting and I/O). The monitor serialises all threads for the duration of that work; contended hand-offs add kernel-level wake-ups, a pattern known as a lock convoy.

**Fix.** Immediate: roll back or disable the audit call, or move it to an asynchronous appender. Permanent: keep only the shared-state update inside the lock, copy what the log needs to a local variable, log after releasing the lock, and prefer a concurrent structure (`LongAdder`, `ConcurrentHashMap.merge`) that needs no external lock.

**Prevention.** Load-test with concurrency equal to production, record lock wait time (JFR event `jdk.JavaMonitorEnter`), and review for I/O or remote calls inside `synchronized` blocks and under `ReentrantLock`.

### Questions to expect

1. **What is the difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore?** A mutex has an owner and must be unlocked by the thread that locked it; a binary semaphore has no owner and can be posted by any thread. Mutexes protect data, semaphores signal events.
2. **When is a spinlock appropriate?** When the critical section is very short, the holder cannot be preempted, and there are at least as many CPUs as contenders, as in kernel code. In user space with more threads than CPUs it collapses because the preempted holder keeps all spinners busy.
3. **Why must a condition variable wait be in a** `while` **loop?** A wake-up does not guarantee the predicate: another thread may consume the state first, and spurious wake-ups are permitted. The loop re-tests the predicate under the mutex.
4. **What is a lost wake-up and how is it prevented?** A signal sent between a waiter's test of the predicate and its sleep is lost. Changing the state and signalling under the same mutex, with `wait` atomically releasing that mutex, prevents it.
5. **What is a futex and why does it make mutexes fast?** A futex is a user-space integer plus a kernel wait queue. Uncontended lock and unlock are atomic instructions on the integer with no system call; the kernel is entered only to sleep (`FUTEX_WAIT`) or to wake (`FUTEX_WAKE`).
6. **How can the producer and consumer deadlock?** If a producer takes the buffer mutex before waiting on the `empty` semaphore, it can sleep holding the mutex while the consumer that would free a slot waits for that mutex.
7. **How is the dining-philosophers deadlock avoided?** By breaking one of the four deadlock conditions: ordering the forks globally (no circular wait), limiting the table to four philosophers with a counting semaphore (one of them can always obtain both forks), or using `tryLock` with back-off (preemption).
8. **What does** `top -H` **show that** `top` **does not?** One line per thread instead of per process, with the thread id that `jstack` and `jcmd` print as `nid`; it identifies the one thread that burns the CPU.
9. **Why can a wider lock lower throughput even below the single-thread rate?** Contended hand-offs involve futex wake-ups and context switches, and the waiters make no progress during the critical section, so extra threads add overhead without parallelism.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A mutex puts waiters to sleep; a spinlock burns CPU and is safe only when the holder cannot be preempted; a semaphore counts and has no owner; a condition variable waits for a predicate, always tested in a loop under the

mutex.

- On Linux, lock state lives in a user-space integer; `futex(FUTEX_WAIT)` and `futex(FUTEX_WAKE)` are the only kernel involvement, and uncontended locking costs about 16 ns with no system call.
- Producer-consumer, readers-writers and dining philosophers each demonstrate one rule: order semaphore waits before the mutex, choose a read-write fairness policy, and impose a global lock order.
- Spin-waiting shows as one thread at 100 percent CPU in `top -H` with `RUNNABLE` in the dump; blocking correctly shows 0 percent.
- Never perform I/O or slow work inside a critical section: it serialises all threads and converts contention into futex traffic.

sections.title: Deadlock, Livelock, Starvation and Priority Inversion

blocks.text:
A set of threads is deadlocked when each thread in the set waits for an event that only another thread in the set can cause. None can proceed, none releases what it holds, and the program stays in that state until it is restarted. A deadlocked server does not crash and does not log an error: its threads are alive and its process is healthy, but requests that reach the affected code never complete. This makes deadlock one of the costliest classes of production defect to detect.

This chapter states the four conditions that make deadlock possible, shows how to represent and detect it, derives the standard prevention and avoidance strategies (including the Banker's algorithm, verified by program), and treats its relatives: livelock, starvation and priority inversion.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The four necessary conditions

Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani showed in 1971 that deadlock can occur only if four conditions hold simultaneously:

- **Mutual exclusion.** At least one resource is held in a non-shareable mode.
- **Hold and wait.** A thread holds at least one resource while waiting for another.
- **No preemption.** A resource can be released only voluntarily by its holder.
- **Circular wait.** A cycle of threads exists in which each waits for a resource held by the next.

The conditions are necessary. For single-instance resources such as locks, a circular wait is also sufficient. Every prevention technique removes one of the four.

blocks.text:
#### Resource-allocation graph

A **resource-allocation graph** has a vertex for every thread and every resource. An edge from a resource to a thread means that the thread holds the resource; an edge from a thread to a resource means that the thread is waiting for it. When every resource has a single instance (a lock), a cycle in the graph is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock. For resources with several instances (a pool, a semaphore with N permits) a cycle is necessary but not sufficient, and a reduction algorithm such as the Banker's safety check is needed.

blocks.text: #### Strategies

rows: Design so that one necessary condition can never hold (global lock order, acquire all at once)
Restricts program structure; may reduce concurrency
Grant a request only if the resulting state is safe (Banker's algorithm)
Needs maximum claims in advance; rarely practical for general locks
Allow deadlock, find the cycle periodically, abort or roll back a victim
Needs a detector and a safe way to abort (databases have both)
Assume deadlock is rare and restart when it happens (the "ostrich algorithm")
Cheap; used by many general-purpose operating systems for user locks
blocks.caption: Four ways to deal with deadlock.

blocks.text:
Linux does not detect deadlocks among user-space mutexes. The kernel has a debugging facility, lockdep, that validates lock ordering of kernel locks, but a deadlock between two application threads is left to the application. The JVM supplies the detector for Java: `jstack`, `jcmd Thread.print` and `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` find cycles among `synchronized` monitors and `java.util.concurrent` locks, as shown in the hands-on section. Database engines run their own detectors on row and table locks.

#### Banker's algorithm

The **Banker's algorithm** (Dijkstra, generalised by Habermann) avoids deadlock for resources with several instances. It requires every process to declare its maximum claim in advance. The system keeps four structures for n processes and m resource types: `Available` (free instances of each type), `Max` (n by m maximum claims), `Allocation` (n by m currently held) and `Need = Max - Allocation`.

A state is **safe** if some order of the processes (a safe sequence) lets each one obtain its remaining need and finish, using what is free plus what earlier processes in the order release. The safety algorithm finds such an order:

1. Set `Work = Available` and mark every process unfinished.
2. Find an unfinished process `i` with `Need[i] <= Work`. If none exists, go to step 4.
3. Set `Work = Work + Allocation[i]`, mark `i` finished and return to step 2.
4. The state is safe if and only if every process is finished.

A request is granted only if it does not exceed the process's declared need, does not exceed `Available`, and the state that would result from granting it is safe. An unsafe state is not yet a deadlock; it is a state from which deadlock cannot be ruled out, so the request is delayed. The algorithm is of limited practical use because processes rarely know their maximum claims and the cost is O(m n squared) per request, but it is the standard exercise that makes the notion of safety precise.

#### Livelock and starvation

In a **livelock** threads are not blocked, yet make no progress because each keeps reacting to the others. The standard example is two threads that each `tryLock` a pair of locks, release the first when the second is unavailable, and retry immediately in lockstep. The remedy is randomised back-off, as used by Ethernet and by well-designed retry loops. In **starvation** a thread is runnable or eligible but is never selected, for example a low-priority thread under a stream of high-priority work, or a writer under a reader-preference lock. Starvation is solved by aging, fair queueing or bounded-waiting protocols; Java offers fair locks (`new ReentrantLock(true)`) at a throughput cost.

#### Priority inversion

**Priority inversion** occurs when a high-priority thread is delayed by a lower-priority one. The basic case is unavoidable and harmless: a high-priority thread waits for a lock briefly held by a low-priority thread. The pathological case arises when a medium-priority thread that does not use the lock preempts the low-priority holder. The high-priority thread now waits not for the holder's short critical section but for the medium thread to finish, which can take arbitrarily long.

blocks.text:
Two protocols bound the delay. In **priority inheritance** the lock holder temporarily runs at the priority of the highest-priority waiter. In the **priority ceiling** protocol each lock has a ceiling equal to the highest priority of any thread that may use it, and the holder runs at that ceiling. POSIX exposes them as `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` and `PTHREAD_PRIO_PROTECT`; on Linux the former is implemented in the kernel by the priority-inheritance futex operations (`FUTEX_LOCK_PI`) and real-time mutexes.

The best-known case is the 1997 Mars Pathfinder mission. As reported by the flight-software team, a low-priority meteorological task held a mutex protecting the shared information bus, a high-priority bus-management task needed the same mutex, and a medium-priority communications task preempted the low-priority holder. A watchdog noticed that the bus-management task had not completed and reset the computer. The cause was found by reproducing the situation on a ground replica with tracing, and the system was repaired by enabling the priority-inheritance option of the VxWorks mutex, which had been available but disabled. The story is cited so often because it shows that the defect lay in a configuration flag and that tracing the real system was what exposed it.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Priority inversion needs strict priorities. Under the default Linux time-sharing policy (EEVDF from kernel 6.6, CFS before) every runnable thread receives CPU time in proportion to its weight, so a medium-weight thread cannot starve a low-weight one indefinitely. The pathological case appears with real-time policies (`SCHED_FIFO`, `SCHED_RR`) and in embedded kernels. Java thread priorities have little or no effect on a default Linux JVM.

### Worked trace

#### Safety check on a concrete state

The state below is the classical five-process, three-resource example: total instances A = 10, B = 5, C = 7. The program `Banker.java` implements the safety algorithm and the request algorithm.

blocks.caption: State of the Banker's example (vectors are A,B,C).

blocks.text: The safety algorithm starts with `Work = (3,3,2)`. P0 does not fit (7,4,3 against 3,3,2); P1 fits (1,2,2), finishes and returns its allocation, giving `Work = (5,3,2)`. The scan continues with P3, P4, P0 and P2, as the figure shows. After P2 the work vector equals the system total (10,5,7), the check that every resource was returned.

blocks.text:
#### Three requests

P1 requests (1,0,2). It does not exceed P1's need (1,2,2) or the available vector (3,3,2). Pretending to grant it yields `Available = (2,3,0)`, P1 allocation (3,0,2) and P1 need (0,2,0); the safety algorithm still finds the sequence P1, P3, P4, P0, P2, so the request is granted. P4 then requests (3,3,0): the first component exceeds `Available = (2,3,0)`, so P4 must wait. P0 requests (0,2,0): the resources exist, but granting leaves `Available = (2,1,0)` and no process has a need that fits, so the resulting state is unsafe and the request is delayed.

blocks.title: Banker.java

blocks.code:
$ java Banker.java
need = [[7, 4, 3], [1, 2, 2], [6, 0, 0], [0, 1, 1], [4, 3, 1]]
initial safe sequence: [1, 3, 4, 0, 2]
P1 requests [1, 0, 2]: granted, safe sequence [1, 3, 4, 0, 2]
P4 requests [3, 3, 0]: must wait, not available
P0 requests [0, 2, 0]: denied, resulting state is unsafe
blocks.title: Banker's algorithm (measured)

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

#### Reproducing a deadlock and reading the dump

The next program is the classical transfer defect: `transfer(from, to)` locks `from` and then `to`. Two threads that transfer in opposite directions acquire the two accounts in opposite orders. The 100 ms sleep stands for slow work (a remote call, a log write) between the two acquisitions and makes the interleaving certain.

blocks.title: TransferDeadlock.java

blocks.text: The program never prints `done`. A process in this state shows no CPU use; both threads are asleep in the kernel on a futex, which `ps -L` confirms by its wait-channel column:

blocks.code:
$ ps -L -o tid,stat,wchan:20,comm -p 14168 | grep -E "TID|transfer"
  TID STAT WCHAN                COMMAND
14187 Sl   futex_do_wait        transfer-A-to-B
14188 Sl   futex_do_wait        transfer-B-to-A
blocks.title: The deadlocked threads at kernel level (measured)

blocks.text: The JVM detector prints the cycle at the end of the thread dump. The section lists, for each thread, the monitor it waits for and its owner, and then the stacks:

blocks.code:
$ jcmd 14168 Thread.print
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"transfer-A-to-B":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x...a0001f70 (object 0x00000000a7b27130, a TransferDeadlock$Account),
  which is held by "transfer-B-to-A"

"transfer-B-to-A":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x...9c0015b0 (object 0x00000000a7b27118, a TransferDeadlock$Account),
  which is held by "transfer-A-to-B"

Java stack information for the threads listed above:
===================================================

blocks.caption: Timeline of the reproduction (the cycle forms at about 100 ms).

blocks.text:
#### Two repairs

The first repair removes circular wait by acquiring the two locks in a global order, here the account identifier. The second removes the unbounded wait by using `tryLock` with a timeout, which lets the caller fail, release what it holds and report an error. The listing contains both and a small test: the ordered version completes 200,000 opposing transfers, and the timed version fails fast when a lock is unavailable instead of hanging.

blocks.title: OrderedTransfer.java

blocks.code:
$ java OrderedTransfer.java
ordered: A=101000 B=-99000 total=2000
timed transfer succeeded = false
blocks.title: Both repairs (measured)

blocks.text:
The balances satisfy conservation (the total stays 2000). The ordered version is the permanent fix because it makes deadlock impossible; the timed version bounds the damage but needs a retry or failure policy and, used alone, can cause livelock when many threads retry in step.

#### Priority inversion on Linux

The program `inv.c` creates three `SCHED_FIFO` threads on one CPU (the process is pinned with `taskset -c 1`): Low (priority 10) takes a mutex and works for 50 ms, High (priority 30) then blocks on the same mutex, and Medium (priority 20) starts a 300 ms busy loop. Real-time policies require privileges, which the build machine provides. The kernel's real-time throttling (`sched_rt_runtime_us`, 950000 per second by default) limits the effect on the rest of the system, and the run is bounded to well under a second.

blocks.title: inv.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -O1 -pthread -o inv inv.c
$ taskset -c 1 ./inv
default mutex       : high-priority thread waited 300 ms for a lock held for 50 ms of work
$ taskset -c 1 ./inv inherit
PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT: high-priority thread waited 49 ms for a lock held for 50 ms of work
blocks.title: Priority inversion and its cure (measured)

blocks.text:
The default run shows 300 ms rather than 350 ms because the 50 ms of Low's work is measured on the wall clock and had already elapsed when Medium finished; the point stands: High waited for Medium's entire run. With `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT`, Low is boosted to priority 30 when High blocks, Medium cannot preempt it, and High waits only for the remainder of Low's critical section.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: a Java deadlock in a payment service

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot payment service exposes `POST /transfers`. The service method locks the source account object and then the destination account object (an in-memory lock used to serialise updates before a batched write). Two customers send money to each other at the same moment.

**Symptoms.** Requests to `/transfers` begin to time out after a deploy; the load balancer marks the instance unhealthy only after its readiness probe, which uses a different code path, also times out on the exhausted thread pool. CPU is at 1 percent, the heap is stable and the log contains nothing at ERROR level. Each timed-out request leaves one more Tomcat worker blocked.

**Diagnosis.** In order: (1) `top -H -p PID` shows no busy thread, so the problem is waiting, not computing. (2) `jcmd PID` `Thread.print > dump.txt` captures the threads; the file ends with `Found one Java-level deadlock`. (3) The report names two threads, the two lock addresses and the owner of each; the source lines in the stacks (`TransferDeadlock.java:12`) point to the second `synchronized`. (4) Every worker that later entered `transfer` is also BLOCKED on one of the same two accounts, which explains the growth. The reproduction in this chapter shows exactly this output; the report in the dump leaves nothing to interpret.

**Root cause.** Circular wait: the lock order depends on the argument order, so opposite transfers acquire the same pair of locks in opposite orders, while the hold-and-wait, mutual-exclusion and no-preemption conditions are satisfied by `synchronized`.

**Fix.** Immediate: restart the instance (a deadlocked JVM never recovers; take the dump first, since it is the evidence). Permanent: acquire the locks in a canonical order (for example by account id), as in `transferOrdered`; or avoid the two-lock design by moving the arbitration to the database with one transaction and `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` in id order. Add a timeout on lock acquisition where an order cannot be imposed.

**Prevention.** Document the lock hierarchy; add a test that runs opposite transfers concurrently with a timeout; run a watchdog that calls `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` every few seconds and reports through the metrics system (a non-null result raises an alert); make the readiness probe exercise the same thread pool as real requests, so that an exhausted pool takes the instance out of rotation quickly.

#### Incident: latency spikes from priority inversion

**Scenario.** A real-time audio gateway (a native service running on a Linux host with `SCHED_FIFO` threads) uses a high-priority thread to deliver samples every 5 ms, a medium-priority thread for packet processing and a low-priority housekeeping thread that updates a shared configuration structure under a mutex also read by the delivery thread. Occasionally the delivery thread misses its deadline by hundreds of milliseconds.

**Symptoms.** Audible gaps without any CPU saturation; the gaps correlate with bursts of packet processing; a watchdog, if present, restarts the service.

**Diagnosis.** Latency tracing (`ftrace` or `trace-cmd` with the scheduler events) is the right instrument. It shows the delivery thread blocked in `futex_wait` while the medium-priority thread runs continuously on the CPU where the housekeeping thread is runnable but not running. In a system without such tools, the reproduction `inv.c` shows the signature: the waiting time of the high-priority thread equals the run time of the medium-priority thread, not the length of the critical section.

**Root cause.** Unbounded priority inversion: an ordinary mutex shared by threads of different real-time priorities.

**Fix.** Immediate: lower the priority of the medium thread or give the housekeeping thread the delivery thread's priority. Permanent: create the mutex with `pthread_mutexattr_setprotocol(PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT)`, as in the second run of `inv.c`, and keep critical sections short.

**Prevention.** Review every mutex shared across real-time priorities; test under load with the medium-priority thread saturated; expose lock wait time as a metric.

#### Incident: an application lock and a database transaction deadlock each other

**Scenario.** A service updates stock inside a database transaction and, within the same transaction, calls a method synchronised on a cache object to refresh the cached stock. Another code path takes the cache lock first and then writes to the database. Neither lock manager sees the other.

**Symptoms.** Occasional requests hang until the database reports a lock-wait timeout (`innodb_lock_wait_timeout` defaults to 50 seconds in MySQL; PostgreSQL's `lock_timeout` is off by default and a statement waits indefinitely). The database deadlock detector reports nothing, because from its point of view one transaction is waiting for a lock held by a transaction that is merely slow. `jcmd Thread.print` reports no deadlock either, because the JVM detector sees only one side.

**Diagnosis.** The thread dump shows one thread BLOCKED on the cache monitor and another RUNNABLE or WAITING inside the JDBC driver (a socket read) while holding that monitor. The database shows a session waiting for a lock and a second session idle in transaction. Matching the two by connection, or by thread name in the log, gives the cycle that crosses both systems. The reproduction below uses SQLite: one thread holds the database write lock and wants the application lock, another holds the application lock and wants the write lock.

blocks.code:
import os, sqlite3, threading, time

DB = "/tmp/osw_o4/mixed.db"
if os.path.exists(DB):
    os.remove(DB)
setup = sqlite3.connect(DB)
setup.execute("CREATE TABLE stock (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, qty INTEGER)")
setup.execute("INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('book', 10)")
setup.commit()
setup.close()

# stands for a synchronized block or ReentrantLock in the service
app_lock = threading.Lock()
t0 = time.time()

def log(who, msg):
    print("%5.2fs  %-8s %s" % (time.time() - t0, who, msg), flush=True)

def tx_then_lock():
    c = sqlite3.connect(DB, timeout=3, isolation_level=None)
    c.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")                       # takes the database write lock
    log("tx-first", "database write lock acquired")
    time.sleep(0.3)
    log("tx-first", "waiting for the application lock")
    with app_lock:                                    # blocks: the other thread holds it
        c.execute("UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1")
    c.execute("COMMIT")

def lock_then_tx():
    c = sqlite3.connect(DB, timeout=3, isolation_level=None)
    with app_lock:
        log("lock-first", "application lock acquired")
        time.sleep(0.3)
        log("lock-first", "waiting for the database write lock")
        try:
            c.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")              # blocks inside SQLite for up to 3 s
        except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:
            log("lock-first", "gave up: " + str(e))

a = threading.Thread(target=tx_then_lock, daemon=True)
b = threading.Thread(target=lock_then_tx, daemon=True)
a.start(); time.sleep(0.05); b.start()
b.join()
log("main", "tx-first still alive after the timeout: %s" % a.is_alive())

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** Two lock hierarchies (application locks and database locks) acquired in opposite orders, with no detector spanning both.

**Fix.** Immediate: kill the stuck database sessions (`KILL`, `pg_terminate_backend`) and restart the blocked instance. Permanent: never hold an application lock while waiting for the database, and never call code that takes an application lock from inside a transaction; derive one global order that includes the database (application lock first, then transaction), or remove the application lock in favour of optimistic concurrency (a version column) and database constraints. Set explicit timeouts at both layers (`lock_timeout`, `innodb_lock_wait_timeout`, `tryLock(timeout)`).

**Prevention.** Alert on sessions idle in transaction for more than a few seconds, on lock waits in the database, and on threads BLOCKED for more than a threshold; set the JDBC and Hikari timeouts below the request timeout so a stuck request fails and releases its resources.

### Questions to expect

1. **State the four necessary conditions for deadlock.** Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. All four must hold; removing any one prevents deadlock.
2. **How do you prevent deadlock among application locks?** Impose a global order on the locks and always acquire in that order (removes circular wait); alternatively acquire all locks atomically, or use `tryLock` with a timeout and back off (removes hold-and-wait or no-preemption).
3. **What is the difference between deadlock, livelock and starvation?** In deadlock threads are blocked forever in a cycle. In livelock they keep running and reacting but make no progress. In starvation a thread is eligible but is never chosen.
4. **Explain a safe state in the Banker's algorithm.** A state is safe if some ordering of the processes lets each obtain its maximum need and finish using the free resources plus those released by earlier processes. An unsafe state may not deadlock, but deadlock cannot be excluded.
5. **How is deadlock detected in a running JVM?** `jcmd PID Thread.print` or `jstack` print "Found one Java-level deadlock" with the cycle; programmatically `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` covers monitors and ownable synchronizers such as `ReentrantLock`.
6. **Can the JVM detector miss a deadlock?** Yes. It does not see threads parked on non-ownable constructs (futures, latches, semaphore waiters), starvation of a thread pool, or cycles that include database or remote locks.
7. **What is priority inversion and how is it solved?** A high-priority thread waits for a lock held by a low-priority thread that a medium-priority thread keeps preempting. Priority inheritance (or ceiling) raises the holder's priority; on Linux this is `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT`.
8. **What happened on Mars Pathfinder?** A low-priority task held the mutex of the information bus, a medium-priority task preempted it, the high-priority bus task missed its deadline and a watchdog reset the computer. Enabling priority inheritance on the mutex fixed it.
9. **How do databases handle deadlocks?** They keep a waits-for graph or use a timeout, choose a victim, roll back its transaction and return an error (SQLSTATE 40P01 in PostgreSQL, error 1213 in MySQL); the application must retry the transaction.
10. **Why is the ordered-lock fix better than a timeout?** Ordering makes the cycle impossible, so no thread ever fails. A timeout only bounds the wait, turns a hang into an error that must be handled, and can cause livelock if retries synchronise.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait; the practical cure is a global lock order, which removes the cycle.
- A resource-allocation graph with a cycle on single-instance locks is deadlock; the JVM reports it in thread dumps as "Found one Java-level deadlock" with owners and stack lines.
- The Banker's algorithm decides whether a request leaves the system in a safe state; the worked example grants P1's request and refuses P0's.
- Priority inversion needs strict priorities; measured, a high-priority thread waited 300 ms for a 50 ms lock until `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` reduced it to 49 ms.
- A cycle that spans application locks and database locks is invisible to both detectors; set timeouts at every layer and never hold an application lock across a database call.

sections.title: Locks in Java and Their Mapping to the Operating System

blocks.text:
Java programs never call `futex` directly, yet every contended `synchronized` block, every `ReentrantLock`, every blocking queue and every `Thread.sleep` ends in the kernel services described in the previous chapters. Understanding the layers explains what a thread dump means, why a thread that waits shows as `S` in `ps`, why a `RUNNABLE` thread may use no CPU at all, and why virtual threads can be blocked by `synchronized` on JDK 21. All traces in this chapter come from OpenJDK 21.0.12 on Linux 6.18.

### Concept and mechanism

#### synchronized and the monitor

Every Java object can serve as a **monitor**: a lock combined with a wait set. The compiler translates a `synchronized` block into the bytecode instructions `monitorenter` and `monitorexit`; a `synchronized` method instead carries the flag `ACC_SYNCHRONIZED` and the JVM acquires the monitor on entry and releases it on exit.

blocks.code:
$ javap -c -p Sync
  void inc();
    Code:
       0: aload_0
       1: dup
       2: astore_1
       3: monitorenter
       4: aload_0
       5: dup
       6: getfield      #7                  // Field count:I
       9: iconst_1
      10: iadd
      11: putfield      #7                  // Field count:I
      14: aload_1
      15: monitorexit
      16: goto          24
      19: astore_2
      20: aload_1
      21: monitorexit
      22: aload_2
      23: athrow
      24: return
    Exception table:
       from    to  target type
           4    16    19   any
          19    22    19   any
blocks.title: Bytecode of a synchronized block (javap -c -p Sync)

blocks.text:
The second `monitorexit` (offset 21) is on the exception path: the exception table covers the body so that the monitor is released even when an exception is thrown. Monitors are re-entrant (the owner can enter again and an entry count is kept), and exit establishes a happens-before edge with the next entry of the same monitor. HotSpot implements the monitor in stages so that the common cases are cheap. The details differ between JDK releases; the following description is the stable outline.

- **Uncontended**: the lock state is recorded in the object header (the mark word) with a compare-and-swap; the owner holds a record on its stack (a thin or lightweight lock). No system call occurs. Biased locking, which removed even the CAS for single-thread use, was disabled by default in JDK 15 and has since been removed.
- **Contended**: when a second thread arrives, the monitor is **inflated** into an `ObjectMonitor` structure in native memory, which holds the owner, an entry list of threads waiting to acquire it and a wait set of threads that called `wait()`. A contender first spins briefly, in the hope that the owner releases soon, and then parks.
- **Deflation**: an idle inflated monitor is deflated back by a background thread (visible in dumps as `Monitor` `Deflation Thread`). **HotSpot object header and monitor: locking escalates as contention appears** CAS contention Thin (stack) lock Inflated (fat) Unlocked mark word points mark word points to mark word: to a lock record in an ObjectMonitor hash, age, 01 What the OS sees: the owner stack in native memory Thin lock: user space only, one CAS. **ObjectMonitor (one per contended object)** Contended: short spin, then the thread parks (futex wait). entry list wait set owner BLOCKED threads WAITING threads thread holding jstack shows BLOCKED waiting to enter after wait() the lock (entry list) or WAITING (wait set). notify(): wait set to entry list Biased locking was disabled in JDK 15 and removed later. monitorexit: pick a successor from the list

*Figure 4.18. The header word escalates from unlocked to a thin lock to an inflated ObjectMonitor;* `BLOCKED` *threads sit in the entry list,* `WAITING` *threads in the wait set, and* `notify()` *moves one from the second to the first.*

`wait()` releases the monitor, adds the thread to the wait set and parks it; `notify()` moves one waiter to the entry list, where it must still compete to reacquire the monitor, which is why `wait()` belongs in a loop that re-tests the predicate (the Java form of the condition-variable rule).

#### ReentrantLock and the AQS framework

`java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock` is implemented in Java on top of `AbstractQueuedSynchronizer` (AQS). The synchronizer keeps an integer `state` (the hold count) and a queue of waiting threads. `lock()` first attempts a CAS on `state`; on failure the thread enqueues a node and calls `LockSupport.park`. `unlock()` decrements the state and, when it reaches zero, unparks the successor in the queue. The class offers capabilities that `synchronized` lacks: `tryLock()` and `tryLock(timeout)` (the basis of the deadlock repair in the previous chapter), `lockInterruptibly()`, an optional **fair** mode that grants the lock in arrival order, and multiple `Condition` objects per lock. `Semaphore`, `CountDownLatch`, `ReentrantReadWriteLock` and `ThreadPoolExecutor`'s worker management are built on the same framework.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Prefer `synchronized` for simple mutual exclusion: it is shorter, cannot be forgotten (no `finally`), and the JVM can optimise it. Use `ReentrantLock` when a timed or interruptible acquire, fairness, or several conditions are required. Always release in `finally`.

#### park and unpark: the bridge to the kernel

Every blocking operation of `java.util.concurrent` reduces to `LockSupport.park()` and `LockSupport.unpark(thread)`. Each Java thread owns a native parker object containing a mutex and a condition variable. `park` waits on that condition variable; `unpark` signals it. glibc implements the condition variable with the futex system call. Consequently, a thread that waits for a `ReentrantLock`, a `Future`, a `BlockingQueue` or a timed sleep is, from the kernel's point of view, a thread in a futex wait.

#### Java thread states against Linux task states

`Thread.getState()` and thread dumps report six states: `NEW`, `RUNNABLE`, `BLOCKED`, `WAITING`, `TIMED_WAITING` and `TERMINATED`. They describe the position of the thread in the Java concurrency model, not the state of the kernel task. In particular `RUNNABLE` means "executing or eligible to execute in the JVM, including blocked in a native call such as a socket read", so a `RUNNABLE` thread may be sleeping in the kernel.

blocks.text:
The practical consequences are direct. A dump with hundreds of `RUNNABLE` threads does not prove CPU saturation; `top` `-H` or the `STAT` and `WCHAN` columns of `ps -L` decide it. A thread that is `BLOCKED` or `WAITING` uses no CPU, so a service with low CPU and high latency is waiting on locks, pools or I/O, which is the premise of the diagnostic procedure in the next chapter.

#### Virtual threads and pinning

JDK 21 made **virtual threads** final (JEP 444). A virtual thread is a Java object scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of platform **carrier threads**, by default a `ForkJoinPool` with as many carriers as CPUs. When a virtual thread blocks in a supported operation (`Thread.sleep`, `ReentrantLock.lock`, socket I/O, `BlockingQueue.take`), it is **unmounted**: its stack is copied to the heap and the carrier is free to run another virtual thread. The kernel sees only the carriers.

A virtual thread is **pinned** when it cannot be unmounted: while it executes inside a `synchronized` block or method, or inside a native method or foreign call. If it blocks while pinned, it blocks its carrier thread in a futex wait like any platform thread. With few carriers, a handful of pinned blocked virtual threads can stall the whole scheduler. JDK 24 removed the `synchronized` case (JEP 491, "Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning"); on JDK 21 and 23 it remains, native frames still pin on later releases, and the flag `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short` prints a stack trace when a thread blocks while pinned.

### Worked trace

#### Following one park and unpark through the kernel

The program `ParkDemo` starts a thread that calls `LockSupport.park()`; the main thread sleeps for 1.5 s, prints a message and calls `LockSupport.unpark`. It was run under `strace -f -tt -e trace=futex,write`, and the lines belonging to the two threads were extracted (timestamps are seconds within one minute; main is thread 3031, the waiter is thread 3054).

blocks.title: ParkDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ strace -f -tt -e trace=futex,write -o park.txt java ParkDemo.java
3054  33.256364 futex(0x7f69384d8220, FUTEX_WAIT_BITSET_PRIVATE|FUTEX_CLOCK_REALTIME, 0, NULL,
                FUTEX_BITSET_MATCH_ANY <unfinished ...>
3031  34.756813 write(1, "main calls unpark\n", 18) = 18
3031  34.756903 futex(0x7f69384d8220, FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE, 1) = 1
3054  34.756918 <... futex resumed>) = 0
blocks.title: Kernel view of park and unpark (typical output, trimmed)

rows: The waiter calls `park`; the parker's condition variable becomes a futex wait on address `0x7f69384d8220` with no timeout (`NULL`). It sleeps for 1.5 s (33.256 to 34.756).
The main thread prints its message (`write`), then calls `unpark`.
`unpark` signals the condition variable: `FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE` on the same address, waking one thread (return value 1).
The waiter's `futex` call returns 0 at 34.756918, 15 microseconds after the wake-up was issued, and the thread resumes in Java.
blocks.caption: Reading the trace.

blocks.text:
The same address on the two calls is the link: the kernel queues the sleeper by address and the wake-up finds it by address. Nothing in the trace is specific to `park`; a contended `synchronized` or `ReentrantLock` produces the same two calls on different addresses.

### Hands-on

#### Observing all six states in one process

`StateDemo` starts seven threads that wait in different ways: a thread holding a monitor while sleeping, a thread blocked on that monitor, one in `Object.wait`, one in `Thread.sleep`, one in `LockSupport.park`, one in `ServerSocket.accept` (on port 20401) and one in a busy loop.

The join key is the number after `nid=`: on JDK 21 it equals the Linux thread id shown by `ps -L` and `top -H`. On JDK 17 and earlier the dump prints it in hexadecimal. The `socket` thread is `RUNNABLE` in Java and sleeping (`S`, `inet_csk_accept`) in the kernel; only the `spinner` is actually running.

#### Virtual-thread pinning

The program starts four virtual threads that each sleep 200 ms while holding a lock, once with a `ReentrantLock` and once with a `synchronized` block (each thread uses its own lock object, so no thread waits for another). The scheduler is restricted to one carrier with `-Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=1` `-Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize=1` to make the effect exact.

$ java -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=1 \
    -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize=1 Pinning.java

  ReentrantLock: 200 ms

    -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize=1 -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short Pinning.java

With the default scheduler on the two-CPU build machine (two carriers) the `synchronized` variant took 400 ms, twice the unpinned time: pinning does not make the program incorrect, it divides the available concurrency by the ratio of blocked pinned threads to carriers.

### Real-world incidents

#### Incident: virtual threads enabled, throughput collapses under load

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot 3.2 service on JDK 21 is switched to virtual threads for request handling (`spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`) to cope with many slow downstream calls. A third-party client library uses `synchronized` around a blocking HTTP call. The pod has a CPU limit of two cores, so the scheduler has two carrier threads.

**Symptoms.** Under moderate load every request that reaches the library is slow, and the service stops responding entirely when two or more concurrent calls to that library are slow: CPU is low, active virtual threads number in the thousands and the platform threads named `ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N` are all blocked.

**Diagnosis.** (1) `jcmd PID Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json` writes a dump that includes virtual threads (the plain `Thread.print` lists only platform threads). (2) `top -H` shows two idle `ForkJoinPool-1-worker` threads, not a busy one. (3) Restart with `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short`: the log prints `reason:MONITOR` with the frame of the `synchronized` block, as in the reproduction. (4) Counting pinned events per minute identifies how often it occurs. The reproduction in this chapter with one carrier shows the quantitative effect: four sleeps of 200 ms took 801 ms instead of 200 ms.

**Root cause.** A blocking call made while holding a monitor pins the virtual thread to its carrier on JDK 21. With as many pinned blocked virtual threads as carriers, no virtual thread can run.

**Fix.** Immediate: restore platform threads (set `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=false`) or raise `-Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize` and `parallelism` as a stop-gap. Permanent: replace the `synchronized` blocks that wrap blocking calls with `ReentrantLock` (own code or a patched library version), or upgrade to JDK 24 or later, where `synchronized` no longer pins; native frames still pin.

**Prevention.** Load-test with virtual threads enabled before release, keep `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short` in the test environment, and monitor the `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` JFR event (it fires when a virtual thread blocks while pinned for longer than a threshold, 20 ms by default).

#### Incident: hundreds of RUNNABLE threads but an idle CPU

**Scenario.** An engineer investigating slow responses takes a thread dump of a Spring Boot service and finds 180 threads in state `RUNNABLE`, most with a stack in `SocketInputStream.socketRead0`. The engineer concludes that the CPU is saturated and requests more cores.

**Symptoms.** Latency is high, `top` reports 5 percent CPU for the process, and adding cores changes nothing.

**Diagnosis.** (1) `top -H -p PID` shows that no thread exceeds a few percent. (2) `ps -L -o tid,stat,wchan:22 -p PID` shows the threads in state `S` with a network wait channel (in the reproduction `inet_csk_accept`; for an established connection a read waits in a socket receive routine). (3) The stack frames show the threads waiting for a downstream service, not computing. The reproduction table in this chapter shows the same contradiction for the `socket` thread: `RUNNABLE` in Java, `S` in the kernel.

**Root cause.** A misreading of `RUNNABLE`, which includes threads blocked in native I/O. The real bottleneck is a slow dependency whose responses the threads are waiting for.

**Fix.** Immediate: none from the service side; reduce the load on the dependency or fail fast. Permanent: set connect and read timeouts, bound concurrency to the dependency with a semaphore or bulkhead, and diagnose the dependency (see the following chapter).

**Prevention.** Teach the three-way comparison of dump state, `top -H` CPU and `ps` state and wait channel; record client-side latency histograms per dependency.

### Questions to expect

1. **How does** `synchronized` **work at the bytecode level?** `monitorenter` and `monitorexit` around the block, with an exception-table entry that releases the monitor on exceptions; for methods the `ACC_SYNCHRONIZED` flag. The monitor is re-entrant.
2. **What happens when a second thread contends for a thin lock?** The monitor is inflated to an `ObjectMonitor`; the contender spins briefly and then parks in the entry list; the owner's release unparks a successor.
3. **How does** `ReentrantLock` **differ from** `synchronized`**?** It is a library class on AQS with `tryLock`, timed and interruptible acquire, optional fairness and several conditions; it must be released in `finally`. Both are re-entrant and give the same memory guarantees.
4. **How do** `park` **and** `unpark` **relate to the kernel?** Each thread has a native parker with a mutex and condition variable; park waits on it and unpark signals it. glibc implements both with `futex` calls, so a parked thread is in state `S` with wait channel `futex_do_wait`.
5. **What is the difference between** `BLOCKED` **and** `WAITING`**?** `BLOCKED` means waiting to enter a monitor held by another thread; `WAITING` means waiting for another thread's action (`wait`, `join`, `park`) with no timeout. `TIMED_WAITING` adds a timeout.
6. **Why can a** `RUNNABLE` **Java thread use no CPU?** `RUNNABLE` includes threads blocked in native calls such as socket reads; the kernel shows them as `S`. Only `top -H` or `ps` state `R` shows a running thread.
7. **What is virtual-thread pinning?** A virtual thread that blocks inside `synchronized` (JDK 21 to 23) or a native frame cannot unmount and occupies its carrier thread; with all carriers pinned the scheduler stalls.
8. **How do you map a thread-dump thread to an OS thread?** Use `nid`: it is the Linux thread id on JDK 21 (hexadecimal on earlier releases); match it with the first column of `top -H` or `ps -L` and with `/proc/PID/task`.
9. **Why must** `wait()` **be called in a loop?** After `notify()` the waiter must reacquire the monitor, and the condition may have changed or the wake-up may be spurious; the loop re-tests the predicate.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- `synchronized` compiles to `monitorenter` and `monitorexit`; HotSpot uses a thin lock when uncontended and an inflated `ObjectMonitor` (entry list and wait set) under contention.
- `ReentrantLock` and every `java.util.concurrent` waiting construct are built on AQS and `LockSupport.park`, which end in `futex(FUTEX_WAIT)` and `futex(FUTEX_WAKE)`.
- Java states are not Linux states: `BLOCKED`, `WAITING` and `TIMED_WAITING` threads are `S` in `futex_do_wait`; `RUNNABLE` may be running (`R`) or blocked in a native call (`S`).
- The `nid` value of a JDK 21 dump equals the Linux thread id seen in `top -H`, `ps -L` and `/proc/PID/task`.
- On JDK 21 a virtual thread that blocks inside `synchronized` pins its carrier; measured with one carrier, four 200 ms sleeps took 801 ms instead of 200 ms.

Concurrency defects rarely announce themselves with an exception. They appear as timeouts, falling throughput, a service that is up but does not answer, or a CPU that is oddly idle or oddly busy. The essential observation that organises the diagnosis is this: a service with high latency and low CPU is waiting, and the question is on what; a service with high latency and high CPU is computing, and the question is where. The instruments for both questions are the thread dump, per-thread CPU, and the kernel's view of each waiting thread.
